warmup.q: A Cassandra cluster has three machines, cass1, cass2 and cass3. cass3 freezes: its program stops for a while and sends nothing at all. With Cassandra 5.0's default settings, about how long until cass1 decides that cass3 is down?
options: About 1 second: the machines talk every second, so one missed message is enough
About 20 seconds: suspicion grows with the silence and passes a threshold after about 18 of the usual gaps
About 3 hours, to be sure it isn't a short hiccup
Never by itself: only a person can mark a machine down
warmup.why: cass1 compares the silence with the usual gap between cass3's heartbeats, the "still here" signals that normally arrive about once a second. Its suspicion, called phi, passes the threshold of 8 after about 18.4 such gaps, and the Try it in the fourth section measured 20 seconds. One missed second is normal wobble, so the first option would raise false alarms all day. The 3 hours is how long Cassandra keeps saved writes for a machine it thinks is down. And a person is needed only to remove a machine from the cluster for good: marking it down is automatic, and each machine does it for itself.

sections.h: No machine in charge: every node keeps its own map of the cluster
sections.html:
Let's put the payments app's account balances into Cassandra. Each balance is one row of a table (a list of records with the same fields), found by its account number, such as A-1001. The lab cluster runs Cassandra on three computers, called cass1, cass2 and cass3. Each computer running Cassandra is a node, and the group is a cluster. Every balance is kept on all three nodes, as three copies called replicas, so one failure loses nothing.

Send a write, a change to a balance, for A-1001 to cass2, and cass2 handles it. The node that takes a request and passes it to the replicas is the coordinator, and any node can be one. So before cass2 does anything, it has to answer two questions alone. Which nodes hold A-1001's copies? And which of them are alive right now?

The obvious design keeps the answers in one place: a master node holds the map, the others ask it, and it decides who is down. HBase, another database program, works that way, and so does Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages, with a small group of machines it calls the KRaft controller (the Consensus track builds one). It costs something. While the master is down or being replaced, nobody learns about changes, and every change passes through one machine.

Cassandra copies a different design, from Dynamo, a system Amazon described in a 2007 paper. Dynamo's rule is symmetry: every node does the same job as every other. So every node keeps its own copy of the whole map. For each node in the cluster, it holds one small record, called that node's endpoint state:

  • its address, and a host ID, a unique name the node picks on its first start
  • its datacenter (a building full of computers) and its rack (a cabinet of computers that share power and a network switch)
  • its 16 tokens, its places on the ring, which the next section explains
  • its state (NORMAL, joining, leaving, shut down) and how much data it holds
  • its Cassandra release, and the version of its schema, the list of tables and their columns

The map is small. A 1,000-node cluster has 16,000 tokens, a few hundred kilobytes of memory. Each node also saves its view in two tables, system.local for itself and system.peers_v2 for everybody else, so it can start from them after a restart.

Back in the office, each clerk is a node, the staff list is the map, and one line on the list is one node's endpoint state. From the map, every node works the rest out alone. Placement is arithmetic: the same map and the same rules give the same replicas on every node, so cass1 and cass3 agree on where A-1001 lives without asking each other. Liveness is different. Each node decides for itself whether a peer is up.

Every node keeps the whole map, and each one judges for itself who is alive.

Next, we'll turn the map into the three nodes that hold one account.

sections.h: From an account number to three nodes: tokens, racks and the snitch
sections.html:
Partitioning: consistent hashing and hot keys built the ring; here's the short version. Murmur3, a hash function (a fixed recipe that turns any text into a number that looks random), turns the account number into a token, a whole number between about minus 9.2 and plus 9.2 billion billion. Bend that range into a circle, like a clock face. Each node owns 16 points on it, its tokens, and a key's copies go to the nodes that own the next tokens clockwise.

That leaves three questions: where a new node puts its tokens, what happens with racks, and how a node knows the racks of the others.

Tokens first. Random points aren't good enough with only 16: in that lesson's demo, one of six nodes got 24.3% of the ring against a fair 16.7%. So Cassandra has a token allocator, switched on in its settings file, cassandra.yaml, by allocate_tokens_for_local_replication_factor: 3. It places a new node's tokens one at a time, each where it brings every node's load closest to the average, counting every copy a node holds. For six nodes, the busiest ends up at 1.02 times the average. A node picks its tokens once, on its first start, so the setting must be right before then.

Then copies. The number of copies is the replication factor (RF), and Cassandra has two rules, called replication strategies, for picking them. SimpleStrategy takes the first RF different nodes clockwise and ignores racks. NetworkTopologyStrategy (NTS) gives each datacenter its own count, such as {'dc1': 3, 'dc2': 3}, and inside each datacenter it spreads the copies over racks. Its rule: walk the ring once; take a node whose rack holds no copy yet; skip a node whose rack already has one, unless the datacenter has fewer racks than copies. In that case, the first (RF minus racks) repeats are taken. The figure walks one key.

A rack is whatever fails together: one power feed and one network switch in a building, or one availability zone, a separate building, in a cloud provider's region. With three racks and RF 3, losing a whole rack still leaves two copies of every row. So QUORUM, a read or write that waits for a majority of the copies (2 of 3), keeps working.

Racks have a trap. One copy per rack means a rack with fewer nodes gives each of its nodes a bigger share. With racks of 2, 2 and 1 nodes and RF 3, the lone node holds a copy of every row; the lab proves it. Keep racks the same size, and grow them together.

Who knows the racks? Each node's snitch, the part of Cassandra that knows where every node sits. GossipingPropertyFileSnitch, which the lab uses and the docs recommend, reads the node's own datacenter and rack from a small file, cassandra-rackdc.properties, and announces them to the others. The snitch also ranks replicas by closeness for reads. Choose the snitch, datacenters and racks before the first write. Changing them later makes Cassandra expect copies on nodes that don't have them, and cassandra.yaml warns that this loses data.

The map is only the same on every node if every change reaches every node. Next, we'll see how the news travels.

sections.h: Gossip: once a second, each node compares notes with one random peer
sections.html:
Every second, every Cassandra node picks another node at random, and the two compare notes. That's the whole protocol (the set of rules the nodes follow), called gossip. It's what the office clerks did on the phone. Every node must hear each change (a node joins with 16 new tokens, a new table appears), and keep hearing that every other node is still alive. That second job uses a heartbeat, a counter each node raises once a second to say "still here".

Version 1: whoever changes tells everyone, and every node sends its heartbeat to every other node once a second. That's N × (N − 1) messages a second for N nodes: 870 for 30 nodes, about a million for 1,000. And a node that misses a message, because it was restarting or the network lost it, never hears that news again.

Version 2: once a second, each node tells one random peer what it knows, and that peer passes it on in its own rounds. News spreads like a rumour: one node knows, then two, then about four. The number that knows roughly doubles every round, so it reaches all N nodes in about log2 N rounds, the number of doublings it takes to reach N (about 10 for 1,000). The demo in the Try it measures a median of 2 rounds for 6 nodes and 8 for 6,000, while a round costs 3 × N messages instead of N². Nothing is lost for good, either: a node that missed the news hears it at its next exchange.

Version 3 shrinks each message. Sending the whole map every second is wasteful when almost nothing changed. So each node keeps one counter, and every heartbeat and every change to its own state takes the next number, its version. Two nodes start by swapping digests, three numbers per node: which node, its generation (below) and its highest version. That's GossipDigestSyn. The receiver replies with GossipDigestAck: the states it has that are newer, plus requests for the ones that are newer at the sender. The sender answers the requests with GossipDigestAck2. Three messages, and only new state travels. The stepper runs it on six nodes.

The generation handles restarts. A restarted node starts its counter from zero, so its versions look older than what the cluster remembers. The generation is the node's start time, in seconds since 1970, and a higher generation wins before versions are compared at all. In the Try it, cass3 came back with a larger generation and heartbeat 32, and every node replaced its old state.

Seeds are contact points. A new node knows nobody, so cassandra.yaml lists a few seeds, and the node asks one of them for the whole map. After that, a seed is an ordinary node that the others gossip with now and then, which keeps the cluster from splitting into groups that never hear each other. One rule matters: a seed never bootstraps, the first-start step where a new node copies its share of data from the others. So a new node must never list itself as a seed, or it joins with no data and answers reads with empty rows.

Gossip tells each node what the others say about themselves. A dead node says nothing at all. Next, we'll see how a node reads silence.

sections.h: Deciding that a node is down: phi turns silence into suspicion
sections.html:
In the Try it below, cass1 marks a frozen cass3 DOWN 20 seconds after it froze. Silence is the only evidence a node has. A frozen program, a dead machine and a cut cable look the same from the other side: newer heartbeats stop arriving. Here the office picture breaks: a clerk knows when a call fails, while a node only notices that no news arrives. (The Faults, time and truth track looks at timeouts in general.)

Version 1 is a fixed timeout: no newer heartbeat for 5 seconds means down. It breaks because heartbeats don't arrive on a schedule. A heartbeat reaches cass1 only when some gossip exchange carries it, so the gaps vary, and they grow across an ocean or when a node is busy. A timeout tight enough for nodes in one building marks healthy nodes down, and up again, on a link between continents. One loose enough for that link is slow to notice a death in one building.

Version 2 learns what normal looks like. That's the phi accrual failure detector, from a 2004 paper by Hayashibara and colleagues, and Cassandra runs a version of it. For every peer, a node keeps the last 1,000 gaps between newer heartbeats, and their average, m. Cassandra assumes each extra moment of silence makes a healthy peer's silence less likely by the same factor, so the chance it stays quiet for t seconds is e^(−t/m). Phi is minus the base-10 logarithm of that chance: phi = t / (m × ln 10), about 0.43 × t/m. In plain words, phi counts zeros: phi 1 means a healthy node is this quiet 1 time in 10, and phi 8 means 1 time in 100 million.

A node convicts a peer, marks it down, when phi passes phi_convict_threshold, 8 by default. In 5.0.9's cassandra.yaml the line is commented out, with the advice that most users never need to change it.

Now the numbers. A heartbeat moves once a second at its source, so on the lab cluster m is about 1 second, and phi crosses 8 after 8 × 2.303 × 1 s = 18.4 seconds of silence (2.303 is ln 10). The check runs once a second, which is how cass1 got to about 20. Two guards keep the detector sane. Gaps longer than 2 seconds are never recorded, so one outage doesn't teach it patience. And a node that was itself frozen for more than 5 seconds marks nobody down. When cass3 woke up, it logged Not marking nodes down due to local pause of 35664433642ns > 5000000000ns (35 seconds, counted in nanoseconds, billionths of a second), because to cass3, everybody had been silent.

A lower threshold would notice a crash sooner, but also mark a healthy node down whenever it's slow for a moment. Akka, a toolkit for building clusters of programs, also uses 8, and suggests 12 on Amazon's rented machines, where gaps vary more.

Down is a local decision, and down isn't gone. UP and DOWN don't travel by gossip: in an earlier freeze on the same cluster, cass2 convicted cass3 half a second before cass1 did. A clean shutdown is announced in gossip, so peers mark that node down within a second, without waiting for phi. And a down node keeps its tokens, because Cassandra never removes a node from the ring unless a person says so. While a coordinator sees cass3 as down, it counts it as missing, sends it no reads, and keeps hints, saved copies of its writes for later delivery, for up to max_hint_window, 3 hours. The stepper follows phi through a freeze.

Next, we'll put the map, the ring and the detector together, and follow one write and one read.

aside.title: Is gossip the only way to keep a list of members?
aside.html: No. SWIM, from a 2002 paper, runs inside tools such as HashiCorp's Consul, which keeps track of which programs run where. Each member pings one random member per round, sending a tiny "are you there?" message, and if no answer comes back, it asks k other members to ping that one for it. News rides on the pings and answers that go out anyway: the paper measured about 2 messages per member per round, whatever the group size, with a failure first noticed after about 1.6 rounds on average. A suspected member can deny it by raising a counter only it may raise, and Lifeguard (HashiCorp, 2017) makes each member stretch its own timeouts when it's slow itself, which cut false alarms more than 50 times in their tests. Cassandra's local-pause guard is a blunt version of that idea.

sections.h: One write and one read, from the account number to the answer
sections.html:
Follow one write of A-2002's balance at QUORUM, sent to cass2. The Try it traces it.

  1. cass2 hashes the partition key, the value that decides where a row lives, here the account number: Murmur3 turns 'A-2002' into the token 1517767796525818520.
  2. It walks its own copy of the ring with NetworkTopologyStrategy. The first token at or after the key is cass3's, the next cass1's, then cass3's again (skipped) and then cass2's. The replicas are cass3, cass1 and cass2, in the order nodetool getendpoints printed.
  3. It asks its failure detector which replicas are up, and compares that with the consistency level, the number of replicas that must answer. QUORUM of three needs two. All three are up, so it goes ahead. With two down, it would answer Unavailable at once and send nothing.
  4. It sends the change, which Cassandra calls a mutation, to every live replica, whatever the consistency level. It writes its own copy the way Wide-column stores with Cassandra described: first to the commit log, a file on disk that every change is added to, then to the memtable, a table in memory. A replica it believes down gets a hint instead.
  5. It answers the client, the program that sent the write, as soon as two replicas have confirmed. In the trace, cass2's own write and cass3's reply made two, and the request finished 0.45 seconds before cass1's reply arrived; cass1 applied the write anyway. If fewer than two replies come back within write_request_timeout, 2 seconds here, the client gets WriteTimeout, and the coordinator keeps hints for the replicas that stayed silent.

A read at QUORUM repeats steps 1 to 3 and then asks fewer nodes. The snitch sorts the live replicas by closeness, the coordinator itself first if it's a replica. The coordinator asks the closest for the data and the next one for a digest, a short hash of its answer. Equal digests end the read. Different ones start a read repair, which fetches the full answers, keeps the newest and fixes the old copy (from the Replication track).

Clients usually save a hop. The Java driver, the library a Java program uses to talk to Cassandra, reads the same map from system.peers_v2 and hears about changes from the node it's connected to. For a prepared statement, a query sent once in advance and then reused, the 4.x driver works out the token itself and sends the request straight to a replica, which coordinates locally. It judges which nodes are up from its own connections; it doesn't run phi.

This design has a limit. Gossip agrees within seconds, not at once, so two nodes can briefly disagree about who is up, or even about who owns a range while a node joins. That's fine for choosing where to send a read, and risky for deciding who owns data. Cassandra 6.0, now in alpha, moves ownership into one ordered log, as the compare box below shows.

refs.title: Apache Cassandra 5.0: Dynamo (tunable consistency, picking consistency levels)

opening:
Picture an office with six clerks and no manager. Each clerk keeps a copy of the staff list: who sits where and who just started. One morning a new clerk arrives, and by lunch every list has her name on it. Nobody sent an email. Every few minutes, each clerk rang one colleague at random, and the two compared lists.

Cassandra, a database program that spreads data over many equal computers, runs the same way. No computer is in charge. It's natural to expect a boss somewhere, one machine that knows who's in the group and who's alive, because most offices and most programs work like that. A boss is simple, right up to the day it's the one that fails.

In Secondary indexes across shards, we asked many shards and waited for the slowest. In this lesson, we'll see how each machine knows the others, where each key lives and who is alive. Then we'll freeze one machine and time how long the others take to notice. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with an office with no manager, where news spread because every clerk rang one colleague at random. Cassandra's nodes do the same once a second, and each one decides alone, from silence, when a peer has been quiet too long: about 20 seconds on the lab cluster.

Next time the lab cluster is up, run nodetool failuredetector on two nodes a few seconds apart, and watch each peer's phi climb and drop back to zero as heartbeats arrive.

Next, we'll set up a Cassandra cluster from its files and settings, add and remove a node, and find out which data moves when the ring changes.

  liveness:  the leader decides who is in, from heartbeats

leader dies   -> election, a few seconds with no metadata changes
every node    -> sees the same order of changes

b.label: Every node keeps it (Cassandra's gossip)
b.title: Every node keeps it (Cassandra's gossip)
b.html:
every node holds the whole map, versioned per node
  changes:   a node bumps its own state's version
  spreading: one random peer a second, Syn / Ack / Ack2
  liveness:  each node runs its own phi detector

any node dies -> nothing to elect; the others carry on
every node    -> converges in about log N rounds, no global order

compare.note: A leader gives one order of changes and one answer to "is this node in the cluster?", and pays with an election, a vote for a new leader, whenever the leader fails. Gossip has no single machine to fail, and costs a little delay and the chance that two nodes briefly disagree: cass1 and cass2 marked cass3 down half a second apart. Cassandra 6.0 (in alpha) moves membership, tokens and schema into a Cluster Metadata Service that puts every change in one log, for exactly that reason, and keeps gossip for heartbeats and load.

lab.title: Build gossip, a phi accrual detector and rack-aware placement
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. They need no Docker. 21 of 22 fail with NotImplementedError. The one that passes checks the given murmur3 against the tokens Cassandra printed in Partitioning: consistent hashing and hot keys.

In PhiAccrual.kt, write heartbeat (record the gap, but never one longer than maxIntervalMillis, and keep at most windowSize gaps) and phi (one line). The six PhiAccrualTest tests pass, including the one that puts conviction at 18.4 seconds.

In Placement.kt, write networkTopology: walk the ring once with the given walk, keep a tally per datacenter (copies wanted, rack repeats allowed, racks used) and follow the rule in the KDoc, the comment above the function. The last test checks you against nodetool getendpoints output captured from the lab cluster.
In Gossip.kt, write examine (the five cases in its KDoc) and apply (generation first, then versions). GossipCluster, which runs rounds of Syn, Ack and Ack2 between your nodes, is given. All 22 pass.
Experiment: in apply, compare versions only and ignore the generation. Run the tests again. The restart tests fail, because a restarted node's small versions lose to its old life. Put it back.
hints: ArrayDeque has addLast and removeFirst. The first heartbeat has no previous one, so it records initialIntervalMillis; the gap check only applies after that.
phi is PHI_FACTOR * (nowMillis - last) / meanMillis. Return 0.0 while lastHeartbeatMillis is null.
For the books, endpoints.groupBy { it.dc } gives each datacenter's nodes; the rack count is nodes.map { it.rack }.toSet().size. HashSet.add returns false when the rack was already there.

In examine, a when with the cases in order reads well: unknown or higher generation there, lower generation there, higher version there, lower version there. local.newerThan(v)!! is safe because you only call it when ours is newer.

In apply, skip ep == name, then replace the whole state when remote.generation > local.generation. With equal generations, merge state by state, keeping the higher version, and report the endpoint when remote.heartbeat > local.heartbeat.

drill.title: The Syn receiver and phi, from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write the body of examine(syn: List<Digest>): Ack for a gossip node whose map is endpoints: Map<String, EndpointState>. Then write the phi formula Cassandra uses, and work out when a peer whose heartbeats arrive on average once a second is marked down.

answer.html: fun examine(syn: List<Digest>): Ack { val requests = mutableListOf<Digest>() val states = sortedMapOf<String, EndpointState>() for (d in syn) { val local = endpoints[d.endpoint] when { // never heard of it, or it restarted: ask for everything local == null || d.generation > local.generation -> requests += Digest(d.endpoint, d.generation, 0) // the sender still has the old life of this node: send everything d.generation < local.generation -> states[d.endpoint] = local.newerThan(0)!! // same life: compare one version number d.maxVersion > local.maxVersion -> requests += Digest(d.endpoint, d.generation, local.maxVersion) d.maxVersion < local.maxVersion -> states[d.endpoint] = local.newerThan(d.maxVersion)!! } } return Ack(requests, states) } // phi = (silence / mean gap) / ln 10, about 0.434 * t / m // convicted when phi > 8: t > 8 * ln 10 * m = 18.4 s for m = 1 s

recap: No Cassandra node is in charge. Every node keeps the whole map of the cluster (tokens, datacenter, rack, state, load, schema) and works out a key's replicas by itself.

Each node owns 16 tokens on the ring, placed by an allocator to within about 2% of even. NetworkTopologyStrategy walks the ring per datacenter and puts one copy in each rack, so keep racks the same size.

Gossip: every second, each node swaps Syn, Ack and Ack2 with one random peer. Versions say what's new, the generation (start time) wins after a restart, and news reaches N nodes in about log2 N rounds. Seeds only introduce new nodes, and a seed never bootstraps.

Phi accrual: phi is about 0.434 × silence ÷ average gap. Past 8, about 18 to 20 seconds on the lab cluster, a node marks a peer down, for itself only. Down means hints and no reads, not removal. SWIM and Lifeguard do the same job with pings, indirect pings and local health.
A coordinator hashes the key, walks its ring, checks live replicas against the consistency level, sends the write to every live replica and answers after enough confirmations.
The limit: gossip agrees within seconds, not at once, so two nodes can briefly disagree about who is up or who owns a range. Cassandra 6.0 moves ownership into one ordered log.

explain.prompt: A friend asks: "If Cassandra has no machine in charge, how does cass2 know where account A-1001 lives and whether cass3 is alive, and how does it learn that a fourth machine just joined?" Answer in a few sentences.
explain.answer: Every node keeps its own copy of the whole cluster map: for each node, its tokens, datacenter, rack, state, load and schema version. Placement is worked out from that map. cass2 hashes A-1001 with Murmur3, walks the token ring clockwise and takes three different nodes, one per rack with NetworkTopologyStrategy, and every node gets the same answer because the map and the rules are the same. Liveness is each node's own call. cass2's phi accrual detector watches how often newer heartbeats from cass3 arrive, and marks it down when the silence is about 18 times the usual gap. The map stays in step through gossip. Every second, each node swaps digests with one random peer (Syn, Ack, Ack2), and only states with newer versions travel. When cass4 joins, it raises the version of its own STATUS and TOKENS, and within a few rounds every node has heard, because the number of nodes that know roughly doubles each round. A restart is recognised by a larger generation, the node's start time.

deeper.html:
Gossip carries more than this lesson used. nodetool gossipinfo on a 5.0 node also shows RPC_READY (the node accepts queries), NET_VERSION, SSTABLE_VERSIONS and, for the local node only, a few old states such as INTERNAL_IP and the old STATUS next to STATUS_WITH_PORT. Since 4.0 every address is sent with its port, so several nodes can share one IP address.

A starting node runs a shadow round before it gossips normally. It sends an empty Syn to its seeds, and they answer with their whole map, so the node can check, for instance, that no live node already uses its address. That is the main thing seeds are for.

The failure detector's local-pause guard exists because a node coming out of a long pause sees every peer silent for, say, 35 seconds. Without the guard it would mark the whole cluster down and flip everyone back to UP a second later. The cap on recorded gaps (cassandra.fd_max_interval_ms, 2 seconds by default, which the startup log mentions as Overriding cassandra.fd_max_interval_ms) keeps an outage from raising the average. The original phi accrual paper assumed gaps follow a bell curve (a normal distribution). Cassandra's exponential assumption makes phi a straight line in the silence, which is what failuredetector showed.

SWIM's suspicion works with an incarnation number, a counter that only the suspected member may raise. When it hears that others suspect it, it raises the counter and gossips that it's alive, and the higher number overrides the suspicion. Lifeguard also lets a suspicion's timeout start long and shrink as other members independently confirm it.

Cassandra 6.0, in alpha, takes membership, tokens and schema away from gossip with Transactional Cluster Metadata (CEP-21). A Cluster Metadata Service on a few nodes puts every change to the ring in one log, so two nodes can't hold different rings, and a join or a removal becomes a sequence of logged steps. Gossip stays for heartbeats and load. The trade is the one in the compare box: one order of changes, in exchange for a small group of nodes that has to be up for the ring to change.

Schema travels by gossip too. Each node gossips SCHEMA, an ID made from its table definitions; a node that sees a different one pulls the schema from that peer, and nodetool describecluster lists every version in the cluster (one, when they agree).

The move away from gossip for ownership is wider than Cassandra. ScyllaDB, a Cassandra-compatible database, switched topology changes to Raft in its 6.0 release, and Kafka 4.0 removed ZooKeeper for its own Raft group. Gossip keeps the job it does well, spreading heartbeats and load cheaply, while ownership of ranges goes to a log that every node reads in the same order.

The snitch has a dynamic part that re-ranks replicas by their measured speed every 100 ms, so reads drift away from a slow copy. The lab cluster switches it off (DynamicEndPointSnitch: disabled in describecluster), so a read stays on the local copy and the traces are easy to follow.

One more way to read this lesson's outputs: nodetool status is a view of gossip (state and load from the map) plus the local failure detector (the U or D), while nodetool ring and describering are pure arithmetic over the tokens in the map.
